implementation_notes: Go's import graph is mechanically checkable and Go forbids cycles at compile time, so its mud is not cyclic — it is a flat set of packages that all import each other, or a small number of packages each containing several subsystems. The compiler surfaces the problem as `go list -deps` output and the classic signal that a package's name stops describing its contents. Consolidation is cheap when the mud is a wide package with many files (Go has no subpackages within a package, so the split requires moving files and renaming references), and the idiomatic boundary is directories as packages with unexported internals.
idiom_name: a few packages with near-complete dependency overlap
pitfalls: Go forbids cycles, so teams solve real coupling by putting shared code in a `util` package — which then becomes the widest package in the system.
Moving a file into a subpackage renames every exported symbol it declared; that compile-error storm is the consolidation cost, and it is one-time.
`go list -deps` grows non-linearly with mud: the fix is measured by the dependency count of the widest package, which is a number worth tracking.
